definition: Eager to learn about things and quick to ask questions.
example: The inquisitive toddler wanted to know why the moon seemed to follow the car.
nuance: Inquisitive stresses actively asking questions; it is often admiring but can hint at prying, while curious stays more neutral.
prompt: A museum guide leads a group of students through a fossil exhibit.
options: One inquisitive student asked how scientists tell how old each bone is.
The inquisitive boy yawned and wandered past every display without a glance.
An inquisitive girl tried to slip a small fossil into her pocket to keep.
Being inquisitive, the student felt sure he knew it all and asked nothing.
reasons: Asking a question to learn more about the fossils shows an active wish to understand.
Ignoring the exhibits shows a lack of interest, the reverse of this trait.
Wanting to own things is being acquisitive, a look-alike word, not asking questions.
Someone with no wish to ask or learn cannot be described this way.

practice.prompt: A new intern spends her first week working at a bakery.
options: The inquisitive frosting on the wedding cake looked delicate and lovely.
The inquisitive intern kept asking the baker why the dough had to rest overnight.
The inquisitive intern never wondered how anything worked and just waited for orders.
The inquisitive intern piled up free pastries until her bag could hold no more.
reasons: Frosting cannot ask questions; the writer has mixed this word up with exquisite.
Repeated questions about how baking works show a strong desire to learn.
Never wondering about anything describes someone incurious, the opposite.
Greedily gathering things fits acquisitive, not a hunger for knowledge.
